moduleTitle: Religious features of the gurdwara: design, furniture and artefacts, including the palki and takht

note.specFocus: Spec 3.1.7.2 Worship and service: religious features of the gurdwara – design, furniture and artefacts; the practices associated with these features and their importance, including the palki and takht.
note.summary:
MEANING
Gurdwara means 'door' or 'gateway to the Guru'. Any building becomes a gurdwara when the Guru Granth Sahib is installed in it. Gurdwaras range from converted houses or churches in Britain to great historic shrines in India.

OUTSIDE
• Nishan Sahib – tall flagpole covered in saffron cloth (chola), with a triangular saffron or blue flag bearing the Khanda; shows that the gurdwara is a place of refuge, food and God's word. The cloth is renewed each Vaisakhi.
• Shoe area and washing facilities – visitors remove shoes and wash hands.
• Many gurdwaras have four doors or entrances (as at the Harimandir Sahib), showing welcome to people from all directions and backgrounds.

THE DIWAN HALL (prayer hall)
• Takht – a raised platform or 'throne' at the front on which the Guru Granth Sahib is placed. It is higher than the sangat, showing the scripture's authority as Guru.
• Palki – a decorated, canopied structure (often like a small palace) on the takht, in which the Guru Granth Sahib is enthroned; 'palki' also refers to the palanquin used to carry the scripture in procession. Shows the Guru's royal status.
• Manji sahib – small cushioned stand/bed on which the Guru Granth Sahib actually rests.
• Chanani – canopy above the scripture, a traditional sign of honour for royalty.
• Rumallas – rich cloths covering the Guru Granth Sahib when not being read; families often offer one at naming or wedding ceremonies.
• Chaur (chaur sahib) – whisk waved over the scripture during reading, a sign of sovereignty and respect.
• Golak – box for offerings.
• No chairs: the sangat sits on the carpeted floor, often men and women on different sides, showing equality and humility. No images or idols.
• Raagis (musicians) sit on a platform to perform kirtan with harmonium and tabla.
• Sachkhand – a separate room where the Guru Granth Sahib is laid to rest at night.

PRACTICES LINKED TO THESE FEATURES
• Prakash – the Guru Granth Sahib is carried (often on the head) to the takht and opened each morning; sukhasan – closed and returned to the sachkhand at night.
• Matha tekna – bowing before the Guru Granth Sahib and making an offering.
• Granthi – reads and looks after the scripture; anyone trained, male or female, may do this.
• Hukamnama – a random reading taken as the Guru's command for the day.
• Karah prasad – sweet blessed food given to all, a sign of God's grace and equality.
• Langar hall – free kitchen (see 2.5).

IMPORTANCE
The features express Guru Gobind Singh's command (1708) that the Granth is the eternal Guru. The scripture is treated as a living sovereign, which focuses worship on God's word. Equality is shown by floor seating, karah prasad and langar.

DIVERSITY
Some gurdwaras are very ornate, others simple; some Sikhs think money is better spent on sewa. Practice varies on seating (some gurdwaras do not separate men and women).

KEY TERMS: gurdwara, Nishan Sahib, Khanda, diwan hall, takht, palki, manji sahib, chanani, rumalla, chaur, golak, sachkhand, prakash, sukhasan, karah prasad.

questions.question:
What is the takht in a gurdwara?
A The flag outside the gurdwara
B The raised platform or throne on which the Guru Granth Sahib is placed
C The whisk waved over the scripture
D The free kitchen
questions.modelAnswer: B – The raised platform or throne on which the Guru Granth Sahib is placed. 'Takht' means throne, showing that the Guru Granth Sahib is treated as a living Guru, like a sovereign. The flag is the Nishan Sahib, the whisk is the chaur and the kitchen is the langar.
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one is correct; write the letter clearly. If unsure, cross out options you know are wrong first.

questions.question:
Which one of the following is waved over the Guru Granth Sahib as a sign of respect and authority?
A Chanani
B Rumalla
C Chaur
D Manji
questions.modelAnswer: C – Chaur (chaur sahib), a whisk usually made of yak hair or nylon set in a handle. In ancient India it was waved over royalty, so waving it over the Guru Granth Sahib shows its sovereign status. The chanani is the canopy, the rumalla the cloth covering and the manji the small bed/stand.
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one is correct; write the letter clearly. If unsure, cross out options you know are wrong first.

questions.question: Give one feature found outside a gurdwara.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: the Nishan Sahib (saffron/blue flag with the Khanda symbol, on a tall pole covered with cloth); a place to remove shoes; a place to wash hands (and sometimes feet); a sign/Khanda emblem; sometimes a pool (sarovar) at historic gurdwaras.
questions.examTip: A 1-mark short response needs one accurate, relevant point only. A short phrase or sentence is enough; do not waste time explaining.

questions.question: Give one practice Sikhs carry out on entering the prayer hall of a gurdwara.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: removing shoes; covering the head; washing hands; walking up to the Guru Granth Sahib and bowing/touching the forehead to the floor (matha tekna); making an offering of money or food; sitting on the floor (often men and women on different sides); not pointing feet towards the Guru Granth Sahib.
questions.examTip: A 1-mark short response needs one accurate, relevant point only. A short phrase or sentence is enough; do not waste time explaining.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which the features of the gurdwara show respect for the Guru Granth Sahib.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: The Guru Granth Sahib rests on the takht or palki, a raised throne, under a chanani (canopy). Placing it higher than everyone else and under a canopy, like a king, shows Sikhs regard it as their living Guru.

Second way: The Guru Granth Sahib is covered with rumallas (decorated cloths) and the chaur is waved over it during reading. These are signs of royalty and care, and each night it is carried with ceremony (sukhasan) to its own room to rest, then opened again in the morning (prakash).
questions.examTip: Give two separate ways. For each, make a simple point (1 mark) and then develop it with an example, consequence or detail (2 marks). Two undeveloped points score only 2.

questions.question: Explain two different ways in which Sikhs show respect when visiting a gurdwara.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: Through their appearance. All visitors, Sikh or not, cover their heads and remove their shoes, and no tobacco or alcohol is allowed. This shows humility before the Guru and treats the gurdwara as a holy place.

Second way: Through their actions before the Guru Granth Sahib. Sikhs walk up to the takht, bow and touch their forehead to the floor (matha tekna), often making an offering, and then sit on the floor without turning their back or feet towards the Guru. This shows the Guru Granth Sahib is the highest authority in their lives.

questions.question:
Explain two features of the gurdwara and their importance for Sikhs.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Sikh belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First feature: The palki and takht. The Guru Granth Sahib is placed on a raised platform (takht), often within a decorated canopied structure (palki), at the front of the diwan hall. Its importance is that it shows the scripture is the living Guru and sovereign, so all worship is directed towards it.

Second feature: The Nishan Sahib. This tall flagpole, covered in saffron cloth and topped with a Khanda, marks every gurdwara. It is important because it shows that the gurdwara is a place where anyone can find shelter, food and God's word, and it represents Sikh identity and the Khalsa.

Source: Guru Gobind Singh declared before his death in 1708 that the Guru Granth Sahib would be the eternal Guru ('Guru Maniyo Granth'). This is why the scripture is enthroned like a ruler on the takht rather than kept on a shelf; the Sikh Rehat Maryada also instructs that it be installed on a clean, raised place under a canopy.
questions.examTip: Explain two teachings, each developed (2 + 2 marks), then name a source of Sikh authority AND apply it to the question (2 marks). Naming the Guru Granth Sahib with an Ang number, or a Guru's teaching, and showing how it supports your point is the safest way to get the source marks.

questions.question:
Explain two practices in the gurdwara associated with the Guru Granth Sahib.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Sikh belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First practice: Prakash and sukhasan. Each morning the Guru Granth Sahib is carried in procession, often on someone's head, from its resting room (sachkhand) to the takht and opened (prakash). In the evening it is closed and returned (sukhasan). This shows Sikhs treat the scripture with the honour due to a living Guru.

Second practice: Taking the hukamnama. After Ardas, the granthi opens the Guru Granth Sahib at random and reads the first hymn on the left-hand page. This is the Guru's 'order' or guidance for the day, which the sangat listens to and tries to follow.

Source: Guru Gobind Singh's command that Sikhs should regard the Granth as Guru ('Sabh Sikhan ko hukam hai, Guru maniyo Granth') explains these practices. Because the Granth is the Guru, Sikhs wake it, put it to rest and seek its command each day, just as followers did with the human Gurus.
questions.examTip: Explain two teachings, each developed (2 + 2 marks), then name a source of Sikh authority AND apply it to the question (2 marks). Naming the Guru Granth Sahib with an Ang number, or a Guru's teaching, and showing how it supports your point is the safest way to get the source marks.

questions.question:
“The palki and takht are the most important features of the gurdwara.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Sikh teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

The palki and takht are where the Guru Granth Sahib is enthroned, and the Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru. Without the scripture, a building would not be a gurdwara ('door of the Guru'). So the place where the Guru sits is the centre of the gurdwara and of all worship.

Everything in the diwan hall is arranged around the takht: the sangat faces it, bows before it and sits lower than it. Rituals such as prakash, sukhasan, Ardas and the hukamnama all happen there. The chanani and chaur that surround it emphasise its royal status, showing the Guru's sovereignty over Sikhs' lives.

Guru Gobind Singh told Sikhs to regard the Granth as Guru (1708), so honouring the Guru's throne is a direct response to his command.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

Many Sikhs would say the langar is equally or more important because it expresses sewa and equality, two central Sikh beliefs. Gurdwaras without a langar are very rare, and it is often the part of the gurdwara most visible to non-Sikhs.

Others might argue that the Guru Granth Sahib itself is what matters, not the furniture. A takht or palki is only a symbol; the scripture could be honoured on any clean raised place. Focusing too much on decoration could risk the kind of ritualism Guru Nanak criticised.

Others again would point to the sangat – the gurdwara exists for the community to meet and remember God (Ang 72). The Nishan Sahib also has importance as a sign of welcome and shelter for all. A non-religious visitor might see the gurdwara's community role, such as food banks and classes, as most important.

CONCLUSION

The palki and takht are the focal point of worship, because they hold the Guru Granth Sahib. But their importance comes entirely from the Guru they support. The best judgement is that the Guru Granth Sahib is the most important thing in the gurdwara, and the palki and takht are the most important features only because they express its status as Guru.
questions.examTip: Use the four bullets: refer to Sikh teaching, argue for the statement, argue for a different view, and reach a justified conclusion. Develop each argument into a chain of reasoning (because... this means... therefore...). Up to 3 extra SPaG marks are available, so use specialist Punjabi terms accurately.

questions.question:
“A gurdwara does not need decoration or special features.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Sikh teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

Guru Nanak criticised religious show and ritual, teaching that truthful living is higher than outward displays (Ang 62). God is present everywhere, so a simple room where the Guru Granth Sahib is respectfully installed and the sangat meets is all that is needed.

Money spent on gold, marble and decoration could instead be used for sewa – feeding the poor or relieving disasters. Many Sikhs admire simple gurdwaras that put their resources into langar and charity.

Elaborate features may create pride (ahankar) or competition between gurdwaras, which feeds haumai rather than removing it. Humanists and other critics might also argue that expensive religious buildings are hard to justify when people are in poverty.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

The special features of the gurdwara are not just decoration – they express beliefs. The takht, palki, chanani, chaur and rumallas show that the Guru Granth Sahib is the sovereign Guru, as Guru Gobind Singh commanded. Without them, it might be treated like an ordinary book.

The Nishan Sahib tells travellers and the community that food and shelter are available, and the langar hall makes sewa and equality possible. Many gurdwaras have four entrances, like the Harimandir Sahib, showing openness to all. These features teach Sikh beliefs visually.

Beauty can inspire devotion. The Harimandir Sahib, covered in gold leaf by Maharaja Ranjit Singh, moves millions of pilgrims spiritually. Offering the best to the Guru can be an expression of love rather than pride.

CONCLUSION

Strictly, a gurdwara only needs the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat; expensive decoration is not required and should never replace sewa. But features such as the takht, chanani, Nishan Sahib and langar are not mere decoration – they express respect for the Guru and Sikh values. So the statement is partly right about decoration, but wrong about special features, which most Sikhs see as important.
evidence: Harimandir Sahib – gold leaf under Maharaja Ranjit Singh
